652.title: First Sunday of Lent
652.hook: the gospel is always the temptation in the desert
652.tomorrow: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)
652.howItsDone: On the First Sunday of Lent the gospel is always the temptation of Jesus in the desert, and in many dioceses the bishop celebrates the Rite of Election for adults preparing for baptism at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday: dust, and Joel's call to tear the inside. Your line was rend your hearts.

The Sunday readings change on a three-year cycle: Matthew one year, Mark the next, Luke the third. Most of the gospels change from one year to the next. But on the first Sunday of Lent, whichever year it is, the story is the same: Jesus, alone in the wilderness, hungry, and tempted. The Church has fixed it there like a signpost at the trailhead. Before you walk the forty days, here's who walked them first, and how it went.
screen: `A THREE-YEAR CYCLE.` → `ONE STORY THAT NEVER MOVES.` → `A SIGNPOST AT THE TRAILHEAD.`

segments.voice: Right after his baptism, the voice from heaven still ringing, the Spirit leads Jesus into the desert. He fasts forty days and forty nights, and afterward, the text says simply, he was hungry. Forty isn't a random number. Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness. Moses stayed forty days on the mountain. Elijah walked forty days to the mountain of God. Jesus steps into the same desert his people knew. Then the tempter comes, three times. First, the hungry man: if thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. He answers from Deuteronomy, in the Douay-Rheims: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." Second, on the pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. Third, on a high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world, his for one act of worship. Each time he answers from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's own desert years. Three temptations, people have noticed, that touch almost everyone: comfort, attention and power. Mark tells it in two verses and adds a detail no other Gospel has: he was with the wild beasts, and the angels ministered to him. On this Sunday, in many dioceses, adults preparing for baptism at Easter are presented to the bishop and enrolled, the Rite of Election. Their forty days begin with his. Lent, in Latin, is Quadragesima, the fortieth. The whole season is shaped like this desert.
screen: `LED INTO THE DESERT.` · `FORTY, THE OLD NUMBER.` · `BREAD, A LEAP, THE KINGDOMS.` · `COMFORT, ATTENTION, POWER.` · then, large: `NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Let it get quiet and ask what your wilderness is right now, a loneliness, a waiting, a craving, a fear, and name it plainly, in one word if you can. Then ask which of the three pulls hardest there, comfort, attention or power, without judging, just naming. If you pray, ask for the angels Mark mentions to minister to you; if not, stay with what you named.
Quadragesima, the fortieth. The Church's Latin name for Lent, the forty days that begin each year with Jesus tempted in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. He walked them first, and the season follows him. That's day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)
653.hook: a feast of Peter's teaching office, not a piece of furniture
653.howItsDone: Catholics keep February 22 as the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, praying for the pope; in Saint Peter's Basilica the altar of the Chair is decorated with candles for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quadragesima: the desert, three temptations, and the forty days. Your line was forty days.

Walk to the far end of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, past the great canopy over the altar, and look up. Floating in a burst of gilded rays, held up by four giant bronze figures, is a chair: a huge, ornate bronze throne by the sculptor Bernini. Tourists photograph it and ask, is that where the pope sits? It isn't. And the feast on February 22 isn't really about a chair either. It's about a word that gave us cathedral.
screen: `THE FAR END OF SAINT PETER'S.` → `A FLOATING BRONZE CHAIR.` → `NOT WHERE THE POPE SITS.`

segments.voice: In the ancient world, a teacher sat to teach. The chair, in Greek and Latin cathedra, was the sign of authority to teach, and a bishop's church is called a cathedral because his chair is in it. So this is a feast of a role, not of furniture: Peter's office of teaching and holding the Church together, which Catholics believe continues in the bishop of Rome. The gospel is Matthew 16. Jesus asks his disciples, who do people say I am? Then, who do you say I am? Simon answers: Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." It's a pun. Peter's new name, Petros in Greek, Kepha in Aramaic, means rock. Christians read this verse differently, and fairly. Catholics see Peter's office as the rock, handed on to his successors. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles but understand that primacy differently. Many Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, or as Christ himself. Inside Bernini's bronze chair is an older wooden one, long honored as Peter's, though it comes from centuries after him. The Church once kept two feasts of Peter's chair, one for Rome and one for Antioch, where tradition says he led the church first; they were combined on this day. And remember who got the name: the same man who would deny knowing Jesus three times. The rock was a man who cracked, and was forgiven.

segments.voice: Catholics pray for the pope today, and if you pray, you can too: for his health, his judgment, his peace. If you don't, choose anyone who has to hold a group together, a parent, a principal, a team lead, a pastor, and sit with what it's like to be the rock others lean on and still a person who can crack. Wish them strength.
Cathedra, the chair. The ancient sign of a teacher's authority, the word behind cathedral, and the reason this feast of Peter's office isn't about furniture. Today's word.
Your line: upon this rock. Tomorrow, a boy who was carried off, and came back. Day six hundred fifty-three, done.

654.title: Saint Patrick (17 March)
654.hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ before me, Christ behind me
654.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 17 as the feast of Saint Patrick, a solemnity and holy day in Ireland; some go to Mass before the parades, and the Breastplate prayer is sometimes sung as a hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cathedra: a teacher's chair, and a pun on rock. Your line was upon this rock.

Green rivers, green beer, plastic hats, a parade down Fifth Avenue. On March 17, people who have never been near Dublin wear green. Ask someone at the parade who Saint Patrick was and you may hear: he drove the snakes out of Ireland and explained the Trinity with a shamrock. Both stories are later legends. In his own writing, Patrick never mentions a snake or a shamrock. He left us something better: his own words, and a prayer that carries his name.
screen: `GREEN RIVERS, GREEN BEER.` → `SNAKES AND SHAMROCKS.` → `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Patrick wasn't Irish. He was born in Britain, tradition says in the fifth century, the son of a deacon, a boy who by his own account didn't take faith very seriously. At about sixteen, raiders from Ireland seized him and sold him as a slave. For six years he herded animals on a cold hillside, and there, alone, he began to pray, he says, a hundred times a day and almost as many at night. Then he escaped, found a ship, and made it home. And years later, he went back, to the people who had enslaved him, as a bishop, to spend his life among them. We know because he wrote it down, in a short Latin work called the Confession, which opens with Patrick calling himself a sinner and very unlearned. Then there's the prayer, called the Breastplate, or the Deer's Cry. Tradition says Patrick sang it while walking past enemies who wanted him dead. It's written in Old Irish, and scholars who study that language place it after his lifetime; tradition gave it his name. Either way, it's a prayer of armor. It calls on the Trinity, then the strength of heaven, sun, fire, sea and rock. Then the famous part: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, beneath me, above me. And it ends looking outward, asking for Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, and in every eye that sees me.
screen: `A BRITISH BOY, ENSLAVED.` · `HE WENT BACK.` · `THE CONFESSION, IN LATIN.` · `THE BREASTPLATE, LATER.` · then, large: `CHRIST IN EVERY EYE THAT SEES ME.`

segments.voice: With each slow breath, notice one direction: in front of you, behind you, to your right, to your left, below, above. If you pray, pray those old lines one direction at a time, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me; if not, simply feel the space around you. Then think of the eyes that will see you today, and the eyes you'll see.

655.title: Saint Joseph (19 March)
655.hook: the silent guardian, patron of the universal Church and workers
655.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 19 as the Solemnity of Saint Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary; in Sicily and in Italian-American communities families set a Saint Joseph's table and share the food with the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Patrick, the enslaved boy who went back. Your line was christ in every eye.

Go through all four Gospels with a highlighter and mark every word Joseph says. You'll finish with a clean highlighter. Mary speaks. The shepherds speak. Joseph, the man who raised Jesus and took him to Egypt and back, never says anything the Gospels record. And yet the Church has made him patron of the whole Catholic Church. Two days after Patrick's parade, the quietest man in the story gets a solemnity.
screen: `A CLEAN HIGHLIGHTER.` → `NOT ONE WORD.` → `PATRON OF THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Matthew introduces him in a crisis. Joseph is betrothed to Mary, and she turns out to be pregnant, and not by him. Under the custom of the time he could have shamed her publicly. Instead, in the Douay-Rheims, Joseph, "being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately." Just, here, means right with God, and his justice comes out as mercy. Then an angel speaks to him in a dream: do not be afraid to take Mary your wife. And Matthew records what he does: "And Joseph rising up from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took unto him his wife." That's the pattern of his whole story. Four times in Matthew, Joseph is told something in a dream, and every time, he gets up and does it. Takes Mary home. Flees to Egypt by night. Comes back. Settles in Nazareth. No speeches. Mark calls Jesus the carpenter, and Matthew the carpenter's son, so it seems Joseph worked with his hands and passed the trade on. The Gospels never mention his death. Tradition says he died before Jesus began preaching, with Jesus and Mary beside him, which is why Catholics call him patron of a happy death. In 1870 Pope Pius IX named him patron of the universal Church: the man who guarded the Holy Family now guards the larger family. In 1955 Pius XII added a second feast, Saint Joseph the Worker, on May 1. And in Sicily, some families still set a Saint Joseph's table today, loaded with bread and sweets, and give it to the poor.

segments.voice: Think of the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid, and choose one task to do carefully, without needing anyone to notice or thank you. Picture doing it the way a good carpenter planes a board: slow, attentive, finished properly. If you pray, ask Saint Joseph to work alongside you; if not, simply give the task your full care.

656.title: The Annunciation (25 March)
656.hook: nine months before Christmas, the Word takes flesh
656.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 25 as the Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord (moved when it falls in Holy Week or the Easter octave), kneel at the Creed's words on the incarnation; the Angelus is traditionally prayed at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Joseph, who says not one word in the Gospels. Your line was the silent saint.

Count back nine months from December 25 and you land on March 25. So in the middle of Lent, with purple on the altar and Easter still weeks off, there's a sudden white solemnity: Christmas, seen from the beginning. By old custom, church bells rang three times a day, at dawn, at noon and at dusk, and people working in the fields stopped and bowed their heads to remember this exact moment. Some churches still ring them.
screen: `NINE MONTHS BEFORE CHRISTMAS.` → `WHITE IN THE MIDDLE OF LENT.` → `BELLS AT DAWN, NOON, DUSK.`

segments.voice: Luke sets it in Nazareth, a town in Galilee. The angel Gabriel comes to a young woman betrothed to Joseph and greets her: hail, full of grace. He tells her she will conceive a son, and call him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. Mary doesn't simply nod. She asks a real question, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the power of the Most High will overshadow her. He tells her that her old cousin Elizabeth, called barren, is six months pregnant. "Because no word shall be impossible with God." And then Mary's answer, the hinge of the story: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, the first word of that last phrase is fiat, let it be done, and Catholics often call this Mary's fiat. It's not passive. She asked, she listened, and she chose. Christians believe that in that moment the Word, who in John's gospel was there in the beginning, took flesh in her. That's why, at Mass today, people kneel at the words of the Creed about the incarnation, as they do on Christmas. And that's what the bells were for. The Angelus, rung morning, noon and evening, walks through this scene in three short lines with a Hail Mary after each: the angel's message, Mary's be it done, and the Word made flesh. A whole Christmas, three times a day, small enough to say in a field.
screen: `GABRIEL IN NAZARETH.` · `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` · `NO WORD IMPOSSIBLE WITH GOD.` · `FIAT: LET IT BE DONE.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: If you pray and know it, pray the Angelus now: three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary. If not, let its shape guide you: first breath, a message arrives; second breath, a question is asked; third breath, a yes is given. Then hold something you've been asked to carry that you didn't plan, and ask whether a yes is possible.
The Annunciation. The angel Gabriel's message to Mary, and her yes, kept on March 25, nine months before Christmas. Today's word.

657.title: Laetare Sunday
657.hook: the rose vestments again, halfway through Lent
657.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Lent the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet, and the entrance antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10, Laetare, Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation: a question, an answer, and Mary's fiat. Your line was be it done.

Anyone who has run a long race knows the halfway marker. Your legs hurt, the excitement of the start line is gone, and the finish is still a long way off. Then a water table, someone on the curb cheering, and you find a little more. Lent has one too. On its fourth Sunday, for one day, the violet gives way to rose. If you were here back in Advent for Gaudete Sunday, you've seen this color before. It shows up only twice a year, and both times it means the same thing.

Laetare is Latin for rejoice, said to one: to a city. It's the first word of the old entrance chant for the fourth Sunday of Lent, from the last chapter of Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all you that love her." Isaiah wrote to people who had mourned Jerusalem's ruin, promising that the city would be like a mother again, nursing and comforting her children. The Church picked that verse for the middle of Lent, when the fasting starts to feel long, the resolutions are wobbling, and Easter is still out of sight. So for one day, the color lightens. Flowers, usually left off the altar in Lent, may come back, and the organ can play more freely. It's sometimes called Mid-Lent Sunday, and in England and Ireland it's also Mothering Sunday, when people once traveled to their mother church, the cathedral or the parish of their baptism; later it became a day to honor mothers too. In some years the gospel is the prodigal son, with a feast for the one who came home. In others it's the man born blind, who sees. Both are stories where the long darkness breaks. Rome kept a custom too: on this Sunday popes would bless a golden rose, an ornament of gold sometimes given to a church or a person as an honor. Gaudete in Advent, Laetare in Lent: each time, the color tells the people in the pews how far they've already come.

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly, as if breathing in something good, fresh air, morning, the smell of rain, and breathe out whatever has felt heavy this Lent, a few times over. Then name one thing you're honestly glad about today, however small, and let it be enough. If you pray, say Isaiah's word, rejoice; if not, let the gladness have a minute.

658.title: Palm Sunday
658.hook: the palms and the long passion read with the whole congregation
658.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, Catholics receive blessed palms, process into church, and hear the Passion read, sometimes in parts with the congregation reading the crowd; some keep the palms at home until next year's Ash Wednesday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laetare, the rose halfway through Lent. Your line was halfway, rejoice.

Ushers stand at the door handing out strips of palm, and within a minute some kid is sword fighting with one, or folding it into a cross. The service begins outside, or at the back, with a procession and singing. Branches wave. It feels like a parade. Then, not long after, the same congregation, holding the same palms, will read aloud a line nobody wants to say. This is a Sunday that turns around in the middle.
screen: `PALMS AT THE DOOR.` →`A PARADE WITH BRANCHES.` → `THE SUNDAY THAT TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the entry. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, a king's entrance done humbly, as the prophet Zechariah had pictured. People throw their cloaks and branches on the road and shout, in Matthew's account in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna is Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. A cry for rescue that had become a shout of welcome. The palms are blessed and the people process, re-enacting it. Then the Mass begins, and the gospel is the Passion, the whole account of his arrest, trial and death, from Matthew, Mark or Luke depending on the year. It's long, and it may be read in parts: a reader narrates, the priest takes the words of Jesus, and the congregation reads the crowd. So the same voices that sang hosanna at the door find themselves saying, together, crucify him. That's deliberate. The Church isn't pointing at a crowd long ago and saying, look what they did. It's handing the line to everyone in the pews. Catholic teaching is clear that the blame for his death falls on all sinners, not on any one people. People take the palms home and tuck them behind a crucifix or a picture, and next year, as Ash Wednesday's lesson told, palms like these become the ashes. This week behind us: forty days, upon this rock, christ in every eye, the silent saint, be it done, halfway, rejoice. Now the week everything has pointed toward.
screen: `A KING ON A DONKEY.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `THE PASSION, IN PARTS.` · `THE PEOPLE READ THE CROWD.` · then, large: `HOSANNA, THEN CRUCIFY.`

segments.voice: If you have a palm from church, find a place for it, behind a crucifix, over a door, tucked into a picture frame; if not, set any green leaf or small branch where you'll see it this week. Sit with it and think how quickly cheering can turn, in a crowd, in a friendship, in yourself. If you pray, say the old cry, hosanna, save, please; if not, simply hold the leaf and the week ahead.
Palm Sunday. The Sunday before Easter: palms and a procession, then the Passion read aloud, with the congregation as the crowd. Today's word.
Your line: hosanna, then crucify. The same mouths, the same week. Day six hundred fifty-eight, done.

chat.says: Why does everyone at Mass say 'crucify him' on Palm Sunday?
options: It's read in parts, and everyone takes the crowd's line: all sinners share the blame.
Only the choir is meant to say it; people just join in when the reader pauses.
It's left over from the palm procession, where the crowd first shouts it at the door.
chat.meaning: The Passion may be read in parts, with the people as the crowd. It hands the line to everyone: Catholic teaching places the blame on all sinners.
